lessons.title: Compare latency orders of magnitude carefully
lessons.summary: Use explicitly hypothetical timing inputs to reason about memory, storage and distance without treating them as benchmarks.
lessons.body:
An estimate should distinguish nanoseconds, microseconds and milliseconds before it chooses an architecture. These examples practise that comparison while keeping their measurement limits explicit.

## Latency numbers every programmer should know

The table below supplies illustrative assumptions for practising unit conversions and comparing orders of magnitude. These are not verified contemporary measurements, and the ratios also vary by hardware and workload.

> [!note] Content gap: latency measurements
> No reproducible hardware/workload record supports this mixed historical latency table. Its values are retained only as hypothetical exercise inputs; benchmark your system before using them for design.

| Operation | Hypothetical exercise time |
|---|---|
| L1 cache reference | 1 ns |
| Branch mispredict | 3–5 ns |
| L2 cache reference | 4–7 ns |
| Mutex lock/unlock | 20 ns |
| Main memory reference | 100 ns |
| Compress 1 KB (Snappy) | 2 µs |
| Send 1 KB over 10 Gbps | 1 µs |
| Random 4 KB SSD read | 20–150 µs |
| Round trip, same datacentre | 0.5 ms |
| Read 1 MB sequentially, SSD | 0.2–1 ms |
| HDD seek | 10 ms |
| Read 1 MB sequentially, HDD | 5–20 ms |
| Round trip, same region (AZs) | 1–2 ms |
| Round trip, London–New York | ~70 ms |
| Round trip, CA–Netherlands–CA | 150 ms |

### What to take away

- Using a 100 µs SSD read from the exercise range, memory is **1,000x faster than SSD** in this comparison, and the assumed in-datacentre round trip costs about as much as several such SSD reads. That's why Redis (in memory, one network hop) is so popular as a cache.
- A **disk seek** costs as much as millions of CPU instructions. Sequential I/O is vastly faster than random I/O, which is why log-structured designs like Kafka and LSM-tree databases are fast at writes.
- **Cross-region round trips are tens to hundreds of milliseconds.** Any design that requires a synchronous cross-region round trip on every write (e.g. synchronous geo-replication) pays this on every request.
- **Chatty protocols are deadly over distance.** 20 sequential calls at 70 ms each = 1.4 s.

## Bulk transfer

> [!example] A lorry full of hard drives
> A lorry carrying 1,000 × 20 TB drives (20 PB) on a 10-hour (36,000-second) drive has enormous throughput: 20 PB delivered in 36,000 s is about 556 GB every second. Its latency is terrible: 10 hours for the first byte. AWS offered exactly this for years: Snowmobile, a lorry-sized container holding up to 100 PB, since retired. Smaller physical-transfer devices use the same principle. AWS stopped accepting new Snowball Edge customers on 7 November 2025 and has announced the end of support for Snowball devices in its commercial Regions on 31 December 2026; check current service availability before choosing a product.

## Key takeaways
- The table supplies exercise assumptions; it is not a reproducible current benchmark.
- Convert timings to the same unit before comparing orders of magnitude.
- Distance and repeated synchronous round trips can dominate designs; validate hardware-specific costs by measuring.

## Further reading
- [Historical latency numbers](https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832)
- [Interactive historical latency numbers](https://colin-scott.github.io/personal_website/research/interactive_latency.html)
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
- [AWS Snowball Edge guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/snowball/latest/developer-guide/)
- [AWS Snowball service availability](https://aws.amazon.com/snowball/)
- [AWS Snow device updates](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/storage/aws-snow-device-updates/)

questions.prompt: Using the lesson's explicitly hypothetical latency numbers, which of these statements are **true**? Select all that apply.

options.text: A main-memory reference is roughly 100× slower than an L1 cache reference
options.explanation: Correct. L1 is ~1 ns and main memory ~100 ns: two orders of magnitude, which is why cache-friendly data layouts matter.

options.text: A round trip within a datacentre (~0.5 ms) is faster than a random 4 KB read from an HDD (~10 ms seek)
options.explanation: Correct. An HDD seek (~10 ms) is about 20× a same-datacentre round trip. That's why reading from a remote machine's RAM can beat reading from local spinning disk.

options.text: A cross-Atlantic round trip is about the same as a random SSD read
options.explanation: Incorrect. London–New York is ~70 ms; a random SSD read is ~20–150 µs. The network round trip is several hundred to thousands of times slower.

options.text: Sequential reads from disk are much faster than random reads
options.explanation: Correct. Random I/O on an HDD pays a ~10 ms seek per access; sequential reads stream at 100+ MB/s. Log-structured systems like Kafka exploit this.

options.text: Network bandwidth improvements have made cross-continent latency negligible
options.explanation: Incorrect. Bandwidth (throughput) has grown enormously, but latency over distance is bounded by the speed of light in fibre (~200,000 km/s). London–New York can't go much below ~60 ms round trip.

questions.workedExample:
Line the numbers up in the same unit (ns):

| Operation | ns |
|---|---|
| L1 | 1 |
| RAM | 100 |
| SSD random 4 KB | ~100,000 |
| DC round trip | 500,000 |
| HDD seek | 10,000,000 |
| London–NY RTT | 70,000,000 |

- RAM / L1 = 100. True.
- DC RTT (0.5 ms) < HDD seek (10 ms). True.
- 70 ms vs 0.1 ms: ~700×, not the same. False.
- Sequential beats random on disk. True.
- Physics sets a floor on the round trip (below). False.

```formula
t = 2 × d / v
t = 2 × 5,570 km / 200,000 km/s
t ≈ 0.056 s = 56 ms
where
t: the minimum round-trip time, there and back, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
d: the one-way distance, London to New York, about 5,570 km
v: the speed of light in fibre, about 200,000 km/s
km: kilometre
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: twice the distance divided by the speed of light in fibre is the fastest any round trip can be, whatever the bandwidth.
```

lessons.title: Translate availability targets into error budgets
lessons.summary: Distinguish availability, reliability and durability, and turn nines into measurable SLO budgets.
lessons.body:
"Is the system up?" sounds like a yes/no question. In practice, availability is a number you design for, measure and trade against cost. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the maths.

## Availability vs reliability vs durability

These words are often used interchangeably. They shouldn't be.

- **Availability**: the fraction of time (or of requests) the system is able to serve correctly. "99.9% of minutes this month the API returned successful responses."
- **Reliability**: the probability the system works correctly *without failure* over a period. A system that fails for 100 ms every minute is 99.8% available but terrible for reliability: almost any long-running job or long-lived connection will hit a failure.
- **Durability**: the probability that stored data is *not lost*. Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability but offers a much lower availability SLA. Data can be safe yet temporarily unreachable.

There are two common ways to turn availability into a number: count time, or count requests.

```formula
A_time = T_up / T_total
A_req = N_ok / N_total
where
A_time: time-based availability, the fraction of time the service was up, from 0 to 1 (multiply by 100 for a percentage)
T_up: the time the service was up and serving correctly during the measurement period, e.g. in minutes
T_total: the length of the whole measurement period, in the same unit as T_up
A_req: request-based availability, the fraction of requests that succeeded, from 0 to 1
N_ok: the number of requests that succeeded in the period
N_total: the total number of requests received in the period
In words: availability is the share of the time, or the share of the requests, for which the service did its job.
```

Example: a 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. A service down for 43 of them has a time-based availability of 43,157 / 43,200 ≈ 0.999, i.e. 99.9%. If it received 1 billion requests and 1 million failed, its request-based availability is 999 million / 1 billion = 0.999, also 99.9%.

> [!note] Time-based vs request-based
> Request-based availability is usually more meaningful for large services (Google SRE favours it), because a 5-minute outage at 3 a.m. affects far fewer users than one at peak.

## The nines

Availability is usually quoted in "nines". Here's the equivalent downtime, using a 365.25-day year and an average month (year/12):

| Availability | Downtime/year | Downtime/month |
|---|---|---|
| 99% (two nines) | 3.65 days | 7.3 hours |
| 99.9% | 8.77 hours | 43.8 min |
| 99.95% | 4.38 hours | 21.9 min |
| 99.99% | 52.6 min | 4.4 min |
| 99.999% | 5.26 min | 26 s |

The formula behind the table: the fraction of time you are allowed to be down is 1 minus the availability.

```formula
D = (1 − A) × T
D = (1 − 0.9999) × 525,960 min
D = 0.0001 × 525,960 min ≈ 52.6 min
where
D: the allowed downtime in the period, in minutes (min)
A: the availability target as a fraction, e.g. 99.99% = 0.9999
T: the length of the period, in minutes; a 365.25-day year is 365.25 × 24 × 60 = 525,960 min
min: minute
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the unavailable fraction multiplied by the length of the period gives the downtime you are allowed.
```

Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10x. The cost of achieving it depends on the architecture and failure modes; there is no universal cost multiplier. At 99.999%, you have 26 seconds a month. Manual detection and recovery can easily consume that budget, so automated recovery is usually essential.

> [!tip] Think in error budgets
> If your SLO is 99.9%, you have a 0.1% **error budget**: about 43 minutes a month. Spend it on deploys, experiments and incidents. When it's gone, slow down releases. This turns availability into an engineering trade-off rather than a moral absolute.

## SLIs, SLOs and SLAs (briefly)

- **SLI** (indicator): the measurement, e.g. proportion of requests returning non-5xx in under 300 ms.
- **SLO** (objective): the target for that SLI, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days.
- **SLA** (agreement): a contract with consequences, e.g. service credits. AWS's EC2 Region-Level SLA specifies 99.99% under its stated multi-AZ deployment and measurement conditions; an individual instance has a separate commitment.

SLAs are normally looser than internal SLOs, so you're warned before you owe customers money. The reliability and observability module goes deeper.

## Key takeaways
- Availability measures successful service, reliability measures failure-free operation, and durability measures retained data.
- Time-based and request-based availability weight partial and peak-hour outages differently.
- An SLI is a measurement, an SLO its target, and an SLA a contractual commitment; the remaining failure allowance is the error budget.

## Further reading
- [Availability table (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/availability-table/)
- [Embracing Risk (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

questions.prompt: Your SLO is **99.9%** availability over a 30-day month. Roughly how much downtime does that allow?

options.text: About 4.3 minutes
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's the budget for 99.99% (four nines). Each extra nine is a 10× reduction, so 99.9% allows ten times more.

options.text: About 43 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. 0.1% of 30 days = 0.001 × 43,200 min = 43.2 minutes.

options.text: About 7.2 hours
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's the budget for 99% (two nines): 1% of 720 hours. You've dropped a nine.

options.text: About 8.8 hours
options.explanation: Incorrect. 8.77 hours is the allowance for 99.9% over a whole **year**, not a month.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
T = 30 × 24 × 60 min = 43,200 min
D = (1 − A) × T
D = (1 − 0.999) × 43,200 min
D = 0.001 × 43,200 min = 43.2 min
where
T: the length of the period, a 30-day month, in minutes (min)
D: the downtime the target allows, in minutes
A: the availability target as a fraction, 99.9% = 0.999
1 − A: the unavailability, the fraction of time you may be down
min: minute
In words: the fraction of time you may be down, multiplied by the minutes in the month, gives the allowed downtime.
```

Quick mental shortcut: 99.9% ≈ 43 min/month, and each additional nine divides by 10 (99.99% ≈ 4.3 min, 99.999% ≈ 26 s).

questions.prompt: An object store advertises 99.999999999% durability and a hypothetical time-based 99.9% monthly availability commitment. A product manager asks: "So we'll basically never be unable to read a file?" What's the accurate answer?

options.text: Yes; eleven nines means effectively always readable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is about data not being *lost*; it says nothing about whether you can reach the data at a given moment.

options.text: Yes, as long as you enable versioning
options.explanation: Incorrect. Versioning protects against accidental overwrites and deletes, not against the service being unreachable.

options.text: No; eleven nines durability means about 1 in 10¹¹ reads will fail
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is measured per object per year (probability of loss), not per read. Failed reads are an availability matter.

options.text: No; durability describes loss risk, while this time-based availability target allows roughly 43 minutes of unavailability in a 30-day month
options.explanation: Correct. The object can be safely stored on many disks yet temporarily unreachable due to network, control-plane or regional problems. The 99.9% SLA is the relevant number for 'can I read it right now?'

questions.workedExample:
Separate the two properties:

| Property | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Durability | Will my data still exist? |
| Availability | Can I access it right now? |

**Durability 99.999999999%:** storing 10 million objects, the advertised design rate corresponds to 0.0001 expected object losses per year, equivalent to one per 10,000 years at that constant rate; it is not a guarantee or a prediction of when a loss occurs.

**Availability 99.9%:** the hypothetical time-based commitment allows about 43 unavailable minutes in a 30-day month. Whether slow requests count depends on the contract's definition of unavailability.

If the product requires reads to be highly available, design for it: cache hot objects, replicate to a second region, or serve via a CDN.

questions.prompt: An API serves a steady 1,000 req/s and has a **request-based** SLO of 99.9% over 30 days. An incident causes 20% of requests to fail for 2 hours. How much of the month's error budget has it used?

options.text: About 278%: 2 hours is far more than the 43-minute budget
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's the time-based view, which treats any degraded minute as fully down. The SLO is request-based, and only 20% of requests failed.

options.text: About 56%
options.explanation: Correct. Budget = 0.1% of 2.592 billion requests ≈ 2.59 million. Failed = 20% × 7.2 million = 1.44 million, which is about 56% of the budget.

options.text: About 20%
options.explanation: Incorrect. 20% is the failure rate during the incident, not the share of the monthly budget consumed.

options.text: About 5.6%
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is off by a factor of 10: check the budget is 0.1% (0.001) of monthly requests, not 1%.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
N = 1,000 /s × 86,400 s × 30
N = 2.592 × 10^9
E = 0.001 × N ≈ 2.592 × 10^6
N_i = 1,000 /s × 7,200 s = 7.2 × 10^6
F = 0.2 × N_i = 1.44 × 10^6
F / E = 1.44 / 2.592 ≈ 0.56
where
N: requests in the 30-day month (86,400 seconds a day)
s: second
10^9, 10^6: a billion and a million (9 or 6 copies of ten multiplied together)
E: the error budget in requests: 1 − 0.999 = 0.001 of the month's requests may fail
N_i: requests during the 2-hour (7,200-second) incident
F: requests that failed, 20% of those
F / E: the share of the month's budget used, about 0.56 = 56%
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the incident failed 1.44 million requests out of an allowance of about 2.6 million, so it spent just over half the month's budget.
```

The team can still ship this month, but cautiously: another incident like this exhausts the budget. Request-based SLOs give partial outages partial weight, which is why Google SRE prefers them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets are **true**? Select all that apply.

options.text: An SLA is normally set looser than the internal SLO for the same service
options.explanation: Correct. The gap means you breach your own objective, and react, before you owe customers credits.

options.text: When the error budget is exhausted, a common policy is to pause risky releases and focus on reliability
options.explanation: Correct. This is the core of an error-budget policy: the budget turns the speed-versus-stability argument into an agreed rule.

options.text: A 100% availability SLO is the ideal target for any user-facing service
options.explanation: Incorrect. 100% is unachievable, users can't tell the difference beyond their own network's reliability, and it leaves no budget for change. Google SRE explicitly argues against it.

options.text: The SLI is the contractual penalty paid when targets are missed
options.explanation: Incorrect. The SLI is the measurement itself (e.g. share of requests succeeding under 300 ms). Penalties belong to the SLA.

options.text: With request-based availability, an outage at peak hour consumes more budget than the same-length outage overnight
options.explanation: Correct. More requests fail at peak, so more of the budget is spent, which matches the real user impact.

questions.workedExample:
Keep the three terms straight:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| SLI | The measurement |
| SLO | Internal target for the SLI |
| SLA | Contract with penalties |

```formula
E = 1 − SLO
E = 1 − 0.999 = 0.001
where
E: the error budget, the fraction of time (or of requests) allowed to fail; 0.001 is 0.1%
SLO: the service level objective, the reliability target as a fraction, here 99.9% = 0.999
In words: whatever the target doesn't promise is yours to spend on change and mishaps.
```

Spend it on releases and experiments; when it's gone, slow down. 100% leaves a budget of zero, so every change becomes forbidden, which is why sensible SLOs are always below 100%.

lessons.title: Model redundancy with capacity and shared failures
lessons.summary: Calculate parallel and two-of-three availability, then test the independence, failover and survivor-capacity assumptions.
lessons.body:
Redundancy helps when another component can take over. Model that benefit using the survivors the workload actually needs, then account for failures that can affect every copy together.

## Components in parallel

If the system works as long as **at least one** of several redundant components works, they're in **parallel**. The system fails only if *all* fail, so work out the chance that every one is down and subtract it from 1:

```formula
A_total = 1 − (1 − A_1) × … × (1 − A_n)
A_total = 1 − ∏(1 − A_i)
where
A_total: the availability of the redundant group, as a fraction from 0 to 1
A_1, A_n: the availability of the first and last (n-th) component, each as a fraction
A_i: the availability of component number i, where i runs from 1 to n
1 − A_1: the unavailability of component 1, the fraction of time it is down
n: the number of redundant components
…: and so on: one factor for every component in between
∏: capital pi, "multiply together": the product of the bracket over every component i; the second line is just a compact way of writing the first
In words: the group is down only when every member is down at once, so multiply their down-fractions and subtract from 1.
```

```
            +--> [App 99%] --+
client ->LB-|                |-> ok
            +--> [App 99%] --+
```

```formula
A = 1 − (1 − A_s) × (1 − A_s)
A = 1 − (0.01 × 0.01)
A = 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999 = 99.99%
where
A: the availability of the pair of app servers, as a fraction
A_s: the availability of one app server, 99% = 0.99, so it is down 1 − 0.99 = 0.01 of the time
In words: two servers that are each down 1% of the time are both down only 1% of 1% of the time.
```

Two 99% servers give 99.99%; three give 99.9999%. Redundancy is enormously powerful, which is why replication across availability zones is standard practice.

> [!warning] Redundancy needs spare capacity
> The parallel formula assumes **one survivor can carry the whole load**. If peak traffic needs both servers, losing either one at peak overloads the other, and the pair behaves like two components in series. Plan for **N+1** (or N+2): enough servers that the system still meets its load with one, or one zone, gone.

When some number of identical servers are needed out of a larger group (written "k of n"), the system is up while at least that many are up. For three 99% servers where any two can carry peak load, add up the chances of the states that work: all three up, or exactly two up.

```formula
P_3 = a^3 = 0.99^3 = 0.970299
P_2 = 3 × a^2 × (1 − a)
P_2 = 3 × 0.99^2 × 0.01 = 0.029403
A = P_3 + P_2 = 0.999702 ≈ 99.97%
where
P_3: the probability that all three servers are up
P_2: the probability that exactly two are up and one is down
a: the availability of one server, 0.99
^: "to the power of": a^3 means a × a × a
3: the number of ways to pick which one of the three servers is the one that is down
A: the availability of the tier, the probability at least two servers are up
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the tier works when all three are up or when exactly one is down; add the probabilities of those two situations.
```

That's a big step down from the 99.9999% you'd get if any *one* could cope, and a big step up from the 97.03% of needing all three.

## The big caveat: independence

The formulas above assume failures are **independent**. In reality, they often aren't:

- Two servers in the same rack share a power supply and switch.
- Replicas running the same software share the same bugs (a bad deploy or a leap-second bug takes them all out at once).
- A bad config push hits every region.
- Failover itself can fail, or take minutes. The parallel formula assumes switching is instant; a 5-minute failover that happens four times a year is 20 minutes of downtime the formula never shows.

Two 99% servers on the same host don't give you 99.99%. This is why cloud providers offer **availability zones** (separate power, cooling and networking) and why multi-region designs exist. It's also why staged rollouts matter: they stop a single bad change from becoming a correlated failure.

> [!warning] Redundancy you haven't tested is a hope, not a design
> A standby database that has never been failed over to is likely to surprise you. Practise failovers regularly (game days, chaos engineering).

## Key takeaways
- Parallel availability improves only when surviving components can serve the required load.
- Two-of-three capacity has different availability from any-one-of-three capacity.
- Shared power, software, config and slow failover invalidate the simplest independent, instant-switch model.

## Further reading
- [Availability and Beyond (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience.html)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: You run three independent app servers behind a load balancer; each is 98% available, and one is enough to serve the traffic. Ignoring the load balancer, what's the availability of the app tier?

options.explanation: Incorrect. 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 = 0.941 is the *series* formula, as if all three had to be up. With redundancy only one needs to be up.
Incorrect. This ignores redundancy entirely. Extra replicas that can each serve traffic raise availability above a single server's.
Incorrect. That's 1 − 0.02 × 0.02, the result for **two** servers. With three, you cube the failure probability.
Correct. The tier fails only if all three are down: 0.02 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 0.000008, so availability is 1 − 0.000008 = 99.9992%.

questions.workedExample:
Parallel formula: the system fails only when **all** fail.

```formula
u = 1 − 0.98 = 0.02
U = u^3 = 0.02^3 = 0.000008
A = 1 − U = 0.999992
where
u: the probability one server is down, 1 minus its 98% availability
U: the probability all three are down at once
^: "to the power of": u^3 means u × u × u
A: the availability of the app tier
In words: three independent servers that are each down 2% of the time are all down together only 8 millionths of the time.
```

So 99.9992%, from servers that are individually only 98%.

Caveat: this assumes failures are independent. If all three share a rack, an AZ, or a bad deploy, the real figure is much lower. That's why replicas are spread across availability zones and deploys are staged.

questions.prompt: Which of these are likely to make real-world availability **lower** than the parallel-redundancy formula predicts? Select all that apply.

options.text: All replicas run in the same rack on the same top-of-rack switch
options.explanation: Correct. A switch or power failure takes out all replicas together: a correlated failure the formula (which assumes independence) doesn't model.

options.text: A config change is pushed to all replicas simultaneously
options.explanation: Correct. A bad config is a common-mode failure that breaks every replica at once, so redundancy provides no protection. Staged rollouts mitigate this.

options.text: Failover takes 3 minutes to detect a failure and promote a standby
options.explanation: Correct. The formula assumes switching is instant. Three minutes of failover per incident is real downtime.

options.text: Replicas are spread across three availability zones
options.explanation: Incorrect. This *reduces* correlation by putting replicas in separate failure domains, bringing reality closer to the formula's prediction.

options.text: All replicas share an identical software bug triggered by a specific date
options.explanation: Correct. Identical software fails identically. Leap-second and date-rollover bugs have taken down whole fleets at once.

questions.workedExample:
The parallel formula for redundant replicas is:

```formula
A = 1 − ∏(1 − A_i)
where
A: the availability of the redundant group
A_i: the availability of replica number i, as a fraction
i: counts through the replicas, 1, 2, 3 and so on
∏: capital pi, "multiply together over every replica i"
In words: the group is down only when every replica is down at once.
```

It assumes:

1. Failures are **independent**.
2. Failover is **instant and always works**.

Check each option against those assumptions:

| Option | Violates |
|---|---|
| Same rack | Independence |
| Global config push | Independence |
| 3-min failover | Instant failover |
| 3 AZs | Neither (it helps) |
| Shared date bug | Independence |

Example: two 99% replicas → formula says 99.99%. If an additional independent shared cause is down 0.5% of the time, on top of the modelled individual failures, it sits in series with the pair:

```formula
A = A_sh × A_pair
A = 0.995 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.9949
where
A: the real availability of the replicated service
A_sh: the availability of the shared cause (a rack switch, say), 99.5% = 0.995
A_pair: the formula's prediction for the pair, 99.99% = 0.9999
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a shared single point of failure caps the pair at roughly its own availability, 99.49% instead of 99.99%.
```

options.text: About 99.9999%, because only one server needs to be up
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's the parallel formula, which assumes one survivor can carry everything. Here one server alone is overloaded at peak.

options.text: About 97.0%, because all three must be up
options.explanation: Incorrect. 0.99 × 0.99 × 0.99 ≈ 97.03% is the probability all three are up, but the tier survives losing one.

options.text: About 99.97%
options.explanation: Correct. The tier is up when at least two are up: the chance all three are up plus the chance exactly two are up, 0.970299 + 0.029403, which is 0.999702.

options.text: About 99.99%, the same as two servers in parallel
options.explanation: Incorrect. Two-in-parallel assumes either one can carry the load alone. This is a 2-of-3 system, a different calculation.

questions.workedExample:
Count the states where at least 2 of 3 are up.

```formula
P_3 = a^3 = 0.99^3 = 0.970299
P_2 = 3 × a^2 × (1 − a)
P_2 = 3 × 0.99^2 × 0.01 = 0.029403
A = P_3 + P_2 = 0.999702
where
a: one server's availability, 0.99
^: "to the power of": a^3 means a × a × a
P_3: the probability all three servers are up
P_2: the probability exactly two are up and one is down
3: the number of ways to choose which server is the one that is down
A: the tier's availability at peak (≈ 99.97%)
In words: add the chance that all three are up to the chance that exactly one is down.
```

Lesson: redundancy only counts if the survivors have the capacity. This is why capacity planning is N+1: size the fleet so it still copes with one server or one zone gone.

questions.prompt: A service runs active-passive across two regions, each 99.9% available, with independent failures and enough standby capacity. The primary region has about **4 incidents a year**, and each failover to the standby (detect, decide, promote, update DNS) takes **15 minutes** of downtime. Roughly what yearly availability should you expect?

options.explanation: Incorrect. The parallel formula assumes instant failover. Here each switch costs 15 minutes, which dwarfs the time both regions are down together.

options.text: Just under 99.99%, about an hour of downtime a year
options.explanation: Correct. 4 × 15 min = 60 min a year from failovers alone. 1 − 60 / 525,960 ≈ 99.989%. The failover time, not the regions' availability, sets the result.

options.text: 99.9%, the same as one region
options.explanation: Incorrect. 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours a year. Failing over in 15 minutes recovers most of that, so the pair does much better than one region.

options.text: 99.8%, because two regions in series multiply
options.explanation: Incorrect. Active-passive regions are redundant, not in series: a request needs only one of them.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
D = n × t_f = 4 × 15 min = 60 min
A = 1 − D / T
A = 1 − 60 min / 525,960 min
A ≈ 0.99989
where
D: yearly downtime from failovers, in minutes (min)
n: failovers per year, 4
t_f: downtime per failover, 15 min
A: the yearly availability (≈ 99.989%)
T: minutes in a 365.25-day year, 525,960
min: minute
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: an hour of failover downtime in a year of 525,960 minutes leaves you just under four nines.
```

The time both regions are down at once is negligible next to this. To improve, cut **MTTR** of the failover itself: automated detection, pre-warmed standby capacity, low DNS TTLs, or active-active so there is nothing to promote.
